holidays.name: National Animal Crackers Day
holidays.description: A day to nibble on the tiny, circus-themed cookies that let you decapitate a lion with zero legal consequences. Folks celebrate by munching on the crunchy critters straight from their iconic box.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial food observance popularized by food-holiday calendars. The cookies themselves trace back to England, where animal-shaped biscuits were imported to the US in the 1870s.
holidays.funFact: Barnum's Animals crackers box, introduced in 1902 by Nabisco, was designed to look like a circus cage, and the string handle was meant for hanging it on a Christmas tree.

holidays.name: International Day for Monuments and Sites
holidays.description: A day dedicated to appreciating the world's old buildings, ruins, and landmarks, from crumbling castles to ancient temples. It is a perfect excuse to hug a historic wall (respectfully).
holidays.origin: Proposed by ICOMOS in 1982 and approved by UNESCO in 1983 to promote awareness of cultural heritage and its preservation.
holidays.funFact: It is also known as World Heritage Day, and UNESCO's World Heritage List includes over 1,100 sites across the globe.

holidays.name: Newspaper Columnist Day
holidays.description: A tribute to the opinionated souls who turn their thoughts, rants, and witty observations into weekly print. Celebrate by reading a column, or by writing a very strongly worded one yourself.
holidays.origin: An unofficial observance said to honor the craft of column writing, tied to the date of the death of journalist Ernie Pyle, a famed WWII columnist, who was killed on April 18, 1945.
holidays.funFact: Ernie Pyle won a Pulitzer Prize in 1944 for his down-to-earth reporting of ordinary soldiers' lives, and his columns ran in hundreds of newspapers.

holidays.name: Great Poetry Reading Day
holidays.description: A day to dramatically read verses aloud to anyone who will listen, including pets, plants, and the unsuspecting barista. Bonus points for a poetic accent or a dramatic pause.
holidays.origin: Established as a literary observance to encourage people to read and share poetry in public and private spaces.
holidays.funFact: Poetry was originally an oral tradition; epic poems like the Iliad were memorized and performed long before they were ever written down.

holidays.name: Paul Revere's Ride Day
holidays.description: A commemoration of the midnight dash by a silversmith on horseback shouting warnings across Massachusetts. Fans celebrate with reenactments, lantern displays, and arguments about what he really yelled.
holidays.origin: Marks the night of April 18, 1775, when Paul Revere and others rode to warn colonists of British troop movements before the battles of Lexington and Concord. Longfellow's 1861 poem made it famous.
holidays.funFact: Revere probably never shouted 'The British are coming!' since colonists still considered themselves British; he more likely said the 'Regulars' were out.
